At first glance, "fast" seems to mean only one thing — quick. But it actually carries two completely separate core ideas, and knowing both will help you understand the word in every situation you'll ever encounter.
Core Idea 1: Speed — Moving or Happening Quickly

This is the most familiar meaning. Something is "fast" when it moves quickly, works quickly, or finishes in a short time.

  • "She is a fast runner." — She runs at high speed.
  • "He has a fast car." — The car can travel very quickly.
  • "That was a fast meeting." — The meeting didn't take long.
  • "This internet connection is very fast." — Pages load quickly.

"Fast" here answers the question: How quickly does it move or happen?

Special case: A fast clock

When a clock or watch is described as "fast," it means it is showing a time that is ahead of the correct time. If it's actually 3:00 but your watch shows 3:07, your watch is seven minutes fast — because it is running too quickly.

  • "My watch is five minutes fast." — It shows a time slightly ahead of the real time.

Common expressions built on the "speed" meaning:

  • Fast food — food that is prepared and served very quickly.
  • Fast-paced — describes something that moves or changes rapidly, like a fast-paced film or a fast-paced city.
  • Fast track — a route to achieving something much more quickly than usual. "She was put on the fast track to promotion."
  • Fast-forward — to move forward through something at high speed, as with a video. Also used figuratively: "Fast-forward to today..."
  • The fast lane — the lane on a road used by the quickest vehicles; also used figuratively for a busy, high-pressure way of life. "She loves living in the fast lane."
Core Idea 2: Firmness — Held Tightly, Fixed, and Secure

This is the meaning most learners don't know, and it is just as real and important. When something is "fast," it can also mean it is firmly held in place — stuck tight, secured, or unable to move.

  • "The boat was fast on the rocks." — The boat was stuck and couldn't move.
  • "Make fast the rope." — Tie/secure the rope tightly. (This is very common in sailing.)
  • "The nail is fast in the wall." — The nail is firmly embedded and won't come out.
  • "Hold fast!" — Don't let go! Keep your grip!
  • "Stand fast." — Hold your position. Do not retreat.

This meaning is especially common in nautical (sailing) language, where sailors "make fast" a rope when they tie it securely to something.
The Most Important Phrases from This "Firmness" Meaning

"Fast asleep"

This is one of the most common uses of "fast" in everyday English, and it trips up many learners. Fast asleep does not mean you fell asleep quickly. It means you are deeply, thoroughly, and completely asleep — so firmly in sleep that you are very difficult to wake up.

Think of it this way: your sleep is solid and secure, just like that nail fast in the wall.

  • "Don't make noise — the baby is fast asleep." (The baby is in a deep, sound sleep.)
  • "He was fast asleep when the phone rang." (He didn't stir at all.)

"Fast friends"

When two people are fast friends, they are very close, deeply loyal, and firmly bonded to each other. The friendship is solid and unshakeable. Again — it does not mean they became friends quickly. It means their friendship is firm and lasting.

  • "They met at university and became fast friends." (Very close, loyal friends.)
Meaning 3: Colors or Dyes That Do Not Fade

A color or dye described as "fast" is one that is permanent — it will not wash out, fade, or run, even after many washes. This connects directly to the "firmness" idea: the color is firmly fixed into the fabric.

  • "Colorfast fabric." — The colors won't fade with washing.
  • "Always use a fast dye for clothes that are washed often."

You will often see this as the single word colorfast, which is very common on clothing labels and product descriptions.

In older English and in classic literature, a "fast" person or "fast" lifestyle describes someone who lives wildly, recklessly, and selfishly in pursuit of pleasure, with no regard for what comes next. You won't hear this in everyday conversation today, but you'll encounter it if you read older novels.

  • "She was known for her fast living." (A reckless, pleasure-filled, irresponsible life.)
  • "He ran with a fast crowd." (He spent time with people who lived wildly.)

Think of it as someone burning through life at high speed — which connects it loosely to the "speed" idea.

"Pull a fast one"

This phrase means to trick or deceive someone, usually by acting quickly before the other person realizes what is happening.

  • "He tried to pull a fast one on me by switching the prices." (He tried to trick me.)

The idea is that the deception happens so fast that the other person doesn't notice until it's too late.
The Big Picture: Holding All of This Together

Here is a simple framework to keep in your mind forever:

"Fast" carries two fundamental ideas:

SpeedMoving or happening quickly
FirmnessFixed, secure, deeply held, unshakeable

Once you know this, nothing about the word will ever confuse you again:

  • Fast car → Speed
  • Fast clock → Running too quickly (speed)
  • Fast asleep → Deeply and firmly asleep (firmness)
  • Fast friends → Close and loyal (firmness)
  • Colorfast / fast dye → Color firmly fixed and won't fade (firmness)
  • Make fast / hold fast → Secure tightly (firmness)
  • Fast living → Wild, reckless lifestyle (speed — burning through life)
  • Pull a fast one → Trick someone before they can react (speed)
